title: LLM-inspired study sheds light on how brain cells encode the meaning of words
source_used: ARY News (Kumail Shah, 11 Oct 2026), the same study; the Medical Xpress original was blocked (HTTP 403)
key_facts: A team from Baylor College of Medicine, Rice University, UC Berkeley and Texas Children's Hospital published a study in Nature Neuroscience on how groups of brain cells store word meanings, borrowing ideas from how large language models (LLMs, the technology behind ChatGPT and Gemini) process text.
The researchers recorded brain activity from 10 people as they listened to stories, using tiny wire electrodes placed temporarily in their brains during routine epilepsy monitoring.
They compared the recordings with word data that AI models produced from the same stories.

Word meanings are stored in complex patterns across many neurons in the hippocampus, a brain area known for memory, and the patterns carry detailed information about how a word's meaning changes with context.
The recorded brain activity matched most closely with data from AI models such as GPT-2.
The team also studied polysemy, where one word has several related meanings, and found that, like AI systems, the brain uses wide networks of neurons to handle context.
The article says the approach could in future help scientists use advanced AI to explore how the human brain works.
quote_evidence: A team from Baylor College of Medicine, Rice University, UC Berkeley, and Texas Children’s Hospital recently published a study in Nature Neuroscience.
The results showed that word meanings are stored in complex patterns across many neurons in the hippocampus, a brain area known for memory.
Interestingly, the brain activity they recorded matched most closely with data from AI models like GPT-2.
why_it_matters_hint: Brain recordings from people line up with how AI language models represent word meaning in context, which gives neuroscientists a new way to test ideas about how the brain handles language.
